# Google Trends search-interest series (agent `data-trends`)

Fetched 2026-10-19T00:41Z .. 2026-10-19T04:19Z. Catalog: `catalog_data-trends.csv` (88 series: 80 weekly, 8 daily). Series files: `series/gt_<term>_w.csv`, `series/gt_<term>_d.csv`. Raw responses: `raw/google_trends/`.

## What was downloaded

Google Trends "interest over time", geography US (`geo=US`), all categories (`category=0`), web search (`property=""`), `hl=en-US`, `tz=300`. Values are Google's 0-100 index: the term's share of all US Google searches in each period, scaled so the maximum of the requested comparison is 100, rounded to integers, with "<1" reported as 0. Every published series is rescaled so its own maximum is 100.

## Access route: what worked and what broke

- Google has no free official bulk API. The Google Trends API (alpha, 2025) needs an approved application; not applied for, as instructed. Everything here uses the public, unofficial web endpoints that the Trends website itself calls. They are unsupported and can change or start blocking at any time.
- Installed from PyPI into `/home/bhoult/programming/c2-wt/venv-data`: `pytrends 4.9.2` (last release 2023), `trendspy 0.1.6` (pulls in `requests 2.34.2`, `pandas 3.0.6`, `numpy 2.5.4`).
- **Used:** my own fetcher (`requests`), replicating trendspy 0.1.6's route, so that pacing, backoff and saving each raw response could be controlled:
  1. `GET https://trends.google.com/trends/embed/explore/TIMESERIES?req={"comparisonItem":[{"keyword","time","geo"}...],"category":0,"property":""}&hl=en-US&tz=300` returns an HTML page with the widget JSON, including its signed `token`, inside `JSON.parse('...')` (hex-escaped).
  2. `GET https://trends.google.com/trends/api/widgetdata/multiline` (one time range) or `.../multirange` (several ranges) with `req=<widget.request>&token=<token>&hl&tz` returns `)]}'`-prefixed JSON (`default.timelineData`).
  - The explore page `https://trends.google.com/trends/explore?geo=US` (fetched once for a session cookie) itself answers HTTP 429 but still sets the `NID` cookie; the embed route worked from the first request.
- pytrends 4.9.2 (`POST /trends/api/explore` then `widgetdata/multiline`), one test call at the end: worked (debt, 2024-01-01..2026-10-17, 146 weekly rows, 2023-12-31..2026-10-11).
- Politeness: strictly one request at a time, 13-18 s (uniform jitter) between any two requests, exponential backoff 60 s -> 15 min on 429. Totals: 595 HTTP requests (incl. 5 probe and 3 pytrends-test requests), 292 saved responses, 5 HTTP 429s, each cleared after a single 60 s backoff. Other failures: 0. Task-level failures: 0.
- Each data response is saved unmodified the moment it arrives (`raw/google_trends/<kind>/...txt`), with a `.meta.json` holding the request items, the widget request, endpoint and fetch time; the runner skips anything already saved, so it can resume. `raw/google_trends/fetch_log.jsonl` logs every request event.

## Discovery: one multirange request = one joint scale (no stitching)

A comparison with the same keyword over several time ranges returns a `fe_multi_range_chart` widget. Its data come back on one joint scale: the maximum over all ranges is 100, and weeks shared by two ranges hold identical values. Checked on a 2-range probe for "debt": range 1 max 39, range 2 max 100, 53 shared weeks identical. Up to 5 ranges per request are accepted, mixed lengths too (1826-day and 1020-day ranges together). So **one request gives a whole 2004-2026 weekly series without stitching** (ranges 2004-01-01..2008-12-31, 2009-01-01..2013-12-31, 2014-01-01..2018-12-31, 2019-01-01..2023-12-31, 2024-01-01..2026-10-17). Range-boundary weeks are reported whole in both ranges; their two values agree to within 1 index point, and I average them. At daily resolution it also works (5 ranges of 261 days come back daily on one scale), but there overlapping ranges are separate samples: shared days agree in scale (median ratio 1.000 on every pair) yet differ by a point or a few (see Repeat pulls). Shared days are averaged.

The cost is integer precision. With one maximum across 22 years, eras of low volume land on 0-5, where the ±0.5 rounding is ±10-100% per value. That matters for spiky terms (one crash or storm week = 100). Single windows (the spec's method) give each 5-year window its own maximum, so where it ran the published series uses it (next section).

## Weekly series: method and stitching error

- **70 weekly series: joint multirange pull** (1 request each, no stitching). The weekly point is labelled with the Sunday that starts the week and covers Sun-Sat. The week starting 2003-12-28 holds only Jan 1-3 2004 and is dropped. The last week used is 2026-10-11..17, which was not flagged `isPartial`.
- **10 weekly series: spec method.** Six overlapping single 5-year windows (2004-01-01..2008-12-31, 2008-01-01..2012-12-31, 2012-01-01..2016-12-31, 2016-01-01..2020-12-31, 2020-01-01..2024-12-31, 2021-10-18..2026-10-17). Each window is rescaled to the previous one by the median ratio over shared weeks where both are >= 5 (if fewer than 8 such weeks: ratio of sums over the overlap; thresholds used at the 50 junctions: >=5 x43, sum x7). The series switches windows at the overlap midpoint, then the whole series is rescaled to max = 100. Terms: debt, dow jones, unemployment, stock market, file for unemployment, flu, heat wave, short selling, margin call, s&p 500.
- **Stitching error**, measured against the independent joint pull (a different request, so it carries its own sampling and rounding). For each window: median over weeks (joint >= 5) of stitched/joint. With perfect stitching these ratios are equal for all windows, so their spread is the accumulated chain error.

The clean estimate comes from terms whose joint pull is precise throughout: gt_debt_w sd 0.5% / max 1.0%, gt_stock_market_w sd 0.5% / max 1.3%.

Median per-window sd over the clean terms: 0.5%. In a `logdiff` series a scale error only enters the moves that span a junction (5 junctions over 22 years); the joint pull has no junctions at all.

## Daily series: method and stitching error

- Daily points exist only for ranges under 270 days. I used a fixed grid of 261-day windows with 45-day overlaps, laid back from 2026-10-17 (39 windows to 2004-01-01). Consecutive windows go into one multirange request (1-5 per request, joint scale) only when the weekly joint series says the group's peak is at most 1.5x each member's own peak, so grouping costs each window at most a third of its precision. Spiky stretches get single windows, calm stretches share a request.
- Requests are chain-stitched over the 45-day overlaps: median ratio where both >= 5 (if fewer than 8 such days: ratio of sums over the overlap, which averages out integer rounding; thresholds used at the 123 junctions: >=5 x111, sum x12), switch at the overlap midpoint, max -> 100. Dates come from `time` (00:00 UTC of the labelled day) and all match `formattedTime`. Day boundaries are Google's.
- Check against the independent weekly joint pull: complete Sun-Sat weeks of each stitched daily series are averaged and compared with the weekly series. The table also shows the per-year drift of the ratio, which is where chain error would accumulate.

Before about 2014, lower-volume terms are dominated by sampling noise at the 1-day horizon, even at similar index levels: Google sampled fewer searches for them. Their daily catalog rows carry a "NOISY BEFORE 2014" flag. For those years use moves of 5 days or more, or the weekly series.


The weekly-logdiff correlation is below 1 because the two pulls are different Google samples with different rounding. Daily series show a day-of-week pattern, with weekends about 20-30% lower than weekdays.

## Repeat pulls (sampling noise)

The 8 key weekly terms were pulled a second time 4-7 minutes later. To force a fresh computation, the second pull shifted every range boundary by 1 day; the weeks returned are the same. For "debt" I also sent an exact repeat.

| term | repeat | t1 -> t2 (UTC) | weeks differing | corr level | corr log | corr weekly logdiff |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| debt | shift1d | 00:48 -> 00:54 | 505/1190 | 0.9967 | 0.9943 | 0.9648 |
| debt | exact | 00:48 -> 00:53 | 505/1190 | 0.9967 | 0.9943 | 0.9648 |
| debt | late | 00:48 -> 02:22 | 506/1190 | 0.9967 | 0.9943 | 0.9648 |
| recession | shift1d | 00:51 -> 00:54 | 2/1190 | 1.0000 | 1.0000 | 1.0000 |
| recession | late | 00:51 -> 02:22 | 2/1190 | 1.0000 | 1.0000 | 1.0000 |
| unemployment | shift1d | 00:51 -> 00:55 | 0/1190 | 1.0000 | 1.0000 | 1.0000 |
| unemployment | late | 00:51 -> 02:23 | 1/1190 | 1.0000 | 0.9999 | 0.9961 |
| stock market crash | shift1d | 00:49 -> 00:55 | 0/1190 | 1.0000 | 1.0000 | 1.0000 |
| stock market crash | late | 00:49 -> 02:23 | 1/1190 | 1.0000 | 1.0000 | 0.9999 |
| bitcoin | shift1d | 00:49 -> 00:56 | 6/1190 | 1.0000 | 0.9984 | 0.9610 |
| bitcoin | late | 00:49 -> 02:24 | 7/1190 | 1.0000 | 0.9983 | 0.9608 |
| inflation | shift1d | 00:52 -> 00:56 | 2/1190 | 1.0000 | 1.0000 | 0.9998 |
| inflation | late | 00:52 -> 02:24 | 5/1190 | 1.0000 | 1.0000 | 0.9997 |
| layoffs | shift1d | 00:52 -> 00:57 | 0/1190 | 1.0000 | 1.0000 | 1.0000 |
| layoffs | late | 00:52 -> 02:25 | 0/1190 | 1.0000 | 1.0000 | 1.0000 |
| buy stocks | shift1d | 00:53 -> 00:57 | 0/1190 | 1.0000 | 1.0000 | 1.0000 |
| buy stocks | late | 00:53 -> 02:25 | 0/1190 | 1.0000 | 1.0000 | 1.0000 |

**Minutes apart, the repeat cannot measure sampling noise.** 7 of 8 terms came back identical or within 1 point in <= 6 weeks (recession, unemployment, stock market crash, bitcoin, inflation, layoffs, buy stocks). Google serves the same sample for a while, and moving the range boundaries by a day does not force a new one: the exact repeat and the shifted pull of "debt" were byte-identical to each other.

For "debt" the sample did change between the first pull (00:48) and the repeats (00:54): 505 of 1190 weeks differ, almost all by 1 index point (peak week 2011-07-24 vs 2011-07-31). Correlation: levels 0.9967, weekly logdiffs 0.965. That is one genuine re-sample of a high-volume term.

**Late repeat, about 1.5 h after the original:** debt 506/1190 weeks differ (corr level 0.9967, weekly logdiff 0.965); recession 2/1190 weeks differ (corr level 1.0000, weekly logdiff 1.000); unemployment 1/1190 weeks differ (corr level 1.0000, weekly logdiff 0.996); stock market crash 1/1190 weeks differ (corr level 1.0000, weekly logdiff 1.000); bitcoin 7/1190 weeks differ (corr level 1.0000, weekly logdiff 0.961); inflation 5/1190 weeks differ (corr level 1.0000, weekly logdiff 1.000); layoffs 0/1190 weeks differ (corr level 1.0000, weekly logdiff 1.000); buy stocks 0/1190 weeks differ (corr level 1.0000, weekly logdiff 1.000).

Late repeat against the 5-minute repeat: debt 1/1190, recession 0/1190, unemployment 1/1190, stock market crash 1/1190, bitcoin 1/1190, inflation 3/1190, layoffs 0/1190, buy stocks 0/1190 weeks differ. So the weekly sample Google served stayed fixed for at least ~1.5 h. The one genuine re-sample in this session is debt's very first pull (00:48), the session's first data request. Weekly sampling noise is therefore best judged from debt's re-sample and from the daily replicates below.

**Daily sampling noise, measured directly** (all years pooled; the by-era table under 'Daily series' is the one to use). Inside one daily multirange request, overlapping ranges share the scale (median ratio 1.000 on every pair) but are separate samples. Over 8418 shared days in 8 terms, the two samples differ by an sd of 2.9-10.0% in log terms (both >= 5). Their 1-day logdiffs correlate 0.236-0.991. So a single daily value carries about 4.5% sampling noise.

## Other data-quality checks

- **Google method changes.** The Trends UI notes data-collection or geo-assignment changes from 2011-01-01, 2016-01-01 and 2022-01-01. Check: median over 48 non-seasonal core terms of the log level change from mid-Oct..Dec to Jan..Feb. In ordinary years it is +6.3% (sd 4.0%). 2011: +11.3%, 2016: +14.5%, 2022: +10.9%. 2016 stands out (a level step of roughly +8% across terms, 2.0 sd). 2011 and 2022 are about 1.2 and 1.2 sd above ordinary years, too little to separate from normal year-to-year variation. In `logdiff` terms this is a one-week jump in the first week of 2016, common to all terms.
- Checked for every series: dates strictly increasing, no duplicate dates, no gaps (weekly = 7 days, daily = 1 day), all values finite and in [0, 100], no sentinels (Trends `-1` "no data" points are dropped before merging), `isPartial` points dropped (none were present). First and last rows were printed and inspected; see `qa_summary` below.
- **Zero handling.** For `logdiff` terms, Trends "<1" (reported 0) is clamped to 0.5 in the units of the request it came from, before rescaling. So the floor is "half the smallest reportable value" of that window, and `log` is always defined. A leading stretch with no measurable volume is cut: the series starts at the first non-zero week from which the next 2 years have < 10% zeros (bitcoin, ethereum, buy bitcoin, tickers listed later, etc.). "crypto" is cut to 2017-01-01: before that it was 0-1 on the joint scale and mostly other senses of the word. Seasonal `anomaly_log1p` terms keep their zeros and are not trimmed.
- **Precision flags** in `notes`: "MOSTLY ZEROS" means > 20% zeros; "LOW PRECISION" means > 50% of points below 5 in source-request units, where the ±0.5 integer rounding dominates week-to-week moves.

## Transforms

- `logdiff` for all non-seasonal terms (values > 0 after the 0.5 clamp).
- `anomaly_log1p` for black friday, flu, coupons, hurricane and heat wave: holiday or weather-season driven, with near-zero levels off-season, so a log change would mostly measure the calendar. Caveats: weekly dates are Sundays, so day-of-year shifts by 1-2 days a year, and Black Friday moves with Thanksgiving (Nov 23-29). The same-day-of-year climatology therefore needs a ±3-day tolerance. "coupons" also has a strong 2009-2012 boom and later decline, so its anomaly carries a trend.
- Annual seasonality was measured for every weekly series as a cross-validated week-of-year R2: a median week-of-year profile of the detrended log level is fitted on odd years and scored on even years, and vice versa. These `logdiff` terms have R2 > 0.25, mostly from the school year and tax season, and are flagged in `notes`: economics 0.84, derivatives 0.83, economy 0.79, housing 0.79, depression 0.76, revenue 0.76, earnings 0.75, gdp 0.74, profit 0.69, jobs 0.63, crisis 0.60, portfolio 0.58, foreclosure 0.53, investment 0.52, inflation 0.51, bonds 0.48, social security 0.48, dividend 0.45, stock market crash 0.45, credit 0.42, sell 0.39, GOOGL 0.34, AMC 0.31, bankruptcy 0.30, AMZN 0.29, stocks 0.28, finance 0.26, JPM 0.25. I kept `logdiff` for them. The spec's `anomaly` is a deviation from earlier years' level, which these trending series would turn into a trend. The test should deseasonalise them or at least be wary of seasonal coincidences.

## Timing (`known_after_days`)

- Weekly: 7. The point dated Sunday D covers D..D+6 (Sat); it is complete after Saturday and visible on Trends by the next day or so, so D+7 (or the first trading day after) is safe.
- Daily: 1, as specified. The day ends at midnight. When fetched, the last day (2026-10-17) and the last week (Oct 11-17) were already final (not `isPartial`) about 1.3 days after they ended. 2 would be the conservative choice for daily if the test wants margin.
- Vintage: these are today's values. Google re-samples, so values seen in real time back then would differ by sampling noise (see repeat pulls). Each series is normalised by its own maximum, which can lie in the future, but that is a pure scale factor and cancels in `logdiff`. The stitch ratios use future weeks only to set the scale of the next window, so they touch only the single move that crosses each junction.

## Terms of use

Google Trends data are public. Google asks that reuse cite "Data source: Google Trends (https://www.google.com/trends)". The endpoints used are not an official API; automated access is subject to Google's Terms of Service. Kept for private research; not redistributed. No account, key or registration was used.

## Not done, and why

- Official Google Trends API (alpha): needs an approved application; not applied for, as instructed.
- Weekly: every requested term was fetched. The monthly all-time fallback was not needed, so none was fetched.
- Spec-method single 5-year windows ran for 10 terms (debt, dow jones, file for unemployment, flu, heat wave, margin call, s&p 500, short selling, stock market, unemployment). Planned but cut by the 3-hour budget: nasdaq, mortgage rates, recession, buy stocks, layoffs, stock market crash. Every other term is published from its joint multirange pull, which has no stitching error but coarser integer precision where volume is low (see the LOW PRECISION flags).
- Hurricane and black friday got no single windows: in every 5-year window one storm or one Black Friday week sets 100, so single windows would not lift their off-peak precision.
- Daily: bitcoin, buy stocks, debt, inflation, layoffs, recession, stock market crash, unemployment. No daily series for other terms (budget).
- Daily series starting after 2004-01: bitcoin from 2011-04-19, buy stocks from 2007-04-02, layoffs from 2006-12-11, recession from 2007-02-15, stock market crash from 2010-09-20. Every planned older daily window was fetched (bitcoin was planned from 2011). These start later because the leading-zero rule (first day from which the next 2 years have < 10% zeros) cut sparse, zero-heavy early years. So gt_stock_market_crash_d has no 2008 crash; that period is only in its weekly series. The raw files for the cut years are kept in raw/google_trends/daily_req/, so a looser trim can be rebuilt with the scripts.
- No other geographies, categories or Google properties (news, YouTube), and no related-queries data: not requested.
